Dear Dr. Mercer,

Thank you for agreeing to see Leo Henderson, a 9-year-old boy referred for a comprehensive diagnostic evaluation.

Leo’s neonatal course was eventful. Delivery followed maternal membranes rupturing prematurely at 35 weeks gestation. On his second day of life, he experienced an acute abdomen secondary to spontaneous perforation of the small bowel, which required emergent laparotomy and repair. During infancy, marked axial and appendicular low tone was evident, leading to clear delays in reaching gross motor milestones; he did not sit independently until 12 months or walk until nearly three years of age.

On examination, Leo demonstrates reduced muscle strength throughout his proximal and distal extremities alongside widespread articular hyperlaxity. His spine exhibits a pronounced kyphoscoliotic alignment. His skin feels remarkably velvety and doughy to the touch, and he displays significant cutaneous hyperextensibility when tested at the forearm and neck. Importantly, his abdominal surgical scar has healed normally, with an absence of spread-out, atrophic scarring or thin, papyraceous scars. Early history and current examination confirm no congenital dislocation of the hips and no clubfoot deformities.

Cardiovascular, respiratory, and cranial nerve examinations are completely normal. Family history is non-contributory; his non-consanguineous parents and older sister are healthy with no history of hyperflexibility or bowel issues. Leo is currently taking no prescription medications, and he enjoys playing adapted soccer.

I would greatly appreciate your specialized assessment and insights into his overall clinical picture.

Best regards,

Dr. Julian Vance
General Pediatrics
